item.title: Contra Oster on Alcohol in Pregnancy. Part 2. Is Europe really superior?
item.description:
In part 1, we established that Oster is likely mistaken as to the mechanism behind FAS/D, and concluded there's no theoretical basis on which to assume there is a threshold effect for problematic drinking in pregnancy, particularly in the first trimester. We also established that risk and BAC were both dependent on weight, which absolute recommendations like "1 drink" don't account for.

In this part, we're going to address the claim that it's reassuring that European nations have both more liberal policies towards drinking in pregnancy and have less FAS/D, citing the so-called "American Paradox," a paper written in 1998 by Ernest L. Abel.

Oster writes:

Think about Europe. Much of the continent is much more permissive about light drinking during pregnancy. Heavy drinking is frowned upon everywhere, but some places in Europe have recommendations suggesting that a few drinks a week are fine. An occasional glass of wine or beer is much more common there. Yet there is no evidence of more fetal alcohol syndrome in Europe; if anything, rates are higher in the United States. If having a couple of glasses of wine a week lowered IQ, we would see big differences between the United States and Europe.*[1]

* As fetal alcohol syndrome is typically a result of binge drinking, it is possible that it could be due to the United States having more inequality in drinking—a lot of people not drinking at all and a few engaging in binge drinking—as opposed to other countries where most people drink moderately.

There are a lot of problems with this besides, namely:

  • It's ecological data which is pretty much the worst possible type of data to draw conclusions from. Ecological data is vulnerable to ecological fallacy amongst other statistical problems.
  • Some European countries used to have more liberal guidance. But by the time Oster was writing, this statement was essentially false; nearly every European country recommended abstinence in pregnancy.
  • We don't actually know if true rates of FAS/D are higher in or lower in individual countries in Europe, let alone Europe as a whole, because there are no universal screening programmes for it in any country, nor many good national prevalence estimates (Oster also mentions average country IQ, which is an even more conflated measure than FAS prevalence rates.)
  • Europe is very heterogeneous in terms of actual drinking prevalence during pregnancy, with some countries drinking more, and some less than the US.

For instance, France is commonly thought by Americans to be liberal about drinking in pregnancy, but France issued abstinence-only advice in 2002, eleven years before Oster published her book. Women in France today report drinking very little in pregnancy, not even light drinking; a survey in 2021 reported 1% of pregnant women having more than 1 drink a month, with 7% having had reported any use. Though the surveys aren't directly comparable due to different methods, surveys of alcohol use in the US report ~15% of women reporting any drinking, and ~4% reporting binge drinking.

The UK, where I live, was one of the very last European countries to change their guidance, and did so after the book came out in 2016. Today (2026) there are a few European countries that don't specifically recommend abstinence in pregnancy, but these countries simply have no guidance published on it at all. All the countries that highlight drinking in pregnancy recommend abstinence.

The ecological fallacy

The canonical example of the ecological fallacy has to do with literacy and immigration. In 1950, statistician William S. Robinson found that the higher percentage of immigrants there were in a state, the lower the illiteracy rate was. This implied that immigrants were more likely to be able to read English than native born Americans!

This is, of course, as Robinson writes, nonsense. When you look at individual level data, immigrants were more likely to be illiterate than native born Americans; it was that immigrants were more likely to settle in big cities in wealthier states. Those wealthier states had lower levels of illiteracy, but a higher proportion of immigrants. Adding in more immigrants just didn't have the power to reverse the direction of the effect. If you look at individual level data, rather than across the state, the correlation is reversed.

Oster clearly is familiar with the ecological fallacy. In her footnotes she gives one plausible example demonstrating this, that the US might have a different distribution of binge drinking, with more binge drinkers than in European countries. But this precise example, of course, supports her argument that light drinking is fine.

This pattern also happens to not be correct, as near as I can tell. I didn't check every country, but i.e. British women are more likely to binge drink than American women in pregnancy, not just drink in general. And French women today both binge in pregnancy less and also do less light drinking in pregnancy too. Per capita, France today consumes more alcohol than the US. But this isn't a paradox, it's simple ecological fallacy. Pregnant women drink less, and non-pregnant women and men drink more. But even though it's not true today, maybe it used to be true in France 30 years ago; let's fine out.

Prevalence of drinking and FAS: today and 30 years ago

It simply isn’t the case that countries with more liberal drinking rules (historically or today) have less FAS, at least that we know of. In reality we just don’t have enough data on it. The very first ever national estimate of prevalence of FAS in France was published in 2021, and only included hospital discharge data, which underestimates prevalence. I wasn't able to find national prevalence estimates in any of the other European countries I looked at (not exhaustive). I found two papers published after Oster that tried to compare country level prevalence; one used models based on alcohol use numbers, not actual diagnosed cases. I did find one slightly more modern paper that tried to (published 2017) with some some real prevalence data, which concluded, "The WHO European Region had the highest prevalence (19.8 per 1000 population; 95% CI, 14.1-28.0 per 1000 population)." However that data still mostly uses estimates.

The reason Oster ended up using a 15 year old paper is plausibly in part because ecological data is widely understood to be inferior to individual level data, so it's a fruitless research direction. And the real prevalence data which might be useful for other reasons that's available just wasn't, and today still isn't, good enough to do this analysis.

So what's wrong with this historical data? The 1998 paper Oster cites references conclusions of Abel's own analysis done in a book. The 1998 paper didn't report these data, but I tracked down the actual data tables that were used to argue this and reanalysed them to make it easier to understand the original analysis. Feeding Claude these data tables, it becomes clear the analysis is very naïve from the outset in a way that should have also been obvious in 1998 and does not support the idea of a paradox.

For one, it didn't even show clear evidence Americans reported drinking less in pregnancy than the rest of the world, even in the early 90s and late 80s. Studies in various American cities run the gamut, with studies in Detroit reporting more drinking in pregnancy than any European city, and Philadelphia, which had less drinking in pregnancy than any European city. If you naively average across studies all with different methods, the confidence intervals overlap substantially. There is only one study from France, Roubaix, and it's middle of the pack at 48.5%. Roubaix was specifically chosen for this study because of high alcohol consumption per capita relative to other cities in France. So we don't know what drinking in France looked like then in general because it's almost certainly not representative. It's possible but would be surprising if a city cherry picked for a higher per capita rate was.

Claude was also asked to read table 11.4 on the relationship between heavy drinking in pregnancy with FAS rate into a CSV and plot them, and do a simple linear regression. Claude in this case reached the same conclusion as the book; no relationship. So Oster's repeating of the hypothesis in the paper of being more heavy drinkers in the US than in "Europe" to explain the "paradox" is contradicted by his own book (the discrepancy might be that the book was under review but not published by the time the paper was. However in itself it's very flawed, because the data aren't independent, caveat emptor.)

In the context of the American paradox, Table 11.4 indicates that the twenty-fold difference in incidence between the United States and other countries cannot be attributed to differences in the number of heavy drinkers at different sites. For example, the rate of heavy drinking in Cleveland, a city with one of the highest rates of FAS, was 1.7%; whereas Boston, with a rate ranging from 2.7% to 13.0%, had only one case of FAS; Australia [Scotland] [2], with a rate of 0.4% to 13.0%, and with an even higher rate of 35.6%, reported no cases.


Looking at the data, I think it's kind of strange the take home story of this data via a game of telephone ended up being was that Europe had less FAS even to begin with.

A striking majority of the studies reported zero cases of FAS, including most of those that took place in the US, with the exception of a few studies of specific cities in the US, France, and Sweden. The studies with no cases were generally small and did not actively screen for FAS, and we usually studying something else (i.e. prevalence wasn't the primary outcome). The sites in the US and France that reported cases were larger, and locations were cherry-picked by looking for places with high alcohol consumption, and the methods used in these studies were active case ascertainment rather than passive case ascertainment. They were simply not intended to estimate country wide prevalence, but to validate screening methods. They were used for prevalence after the fact. Nevertheless two Sokol papers with the highest rates were still not statistically distinguishable from nearly all of the European studies due to overlapping confidence intervals. It took pooling to do that.

Table 11.1 notes race and SES/class for each study, but those weren't used in the analysis. The data is analysed raw, with little attempt to statistically control for methodology, SES, or race, or region. Instead, Abel simply pooled all the cases together.

If you look at the pooled data in table 11.1, from which Abel concludes the US has 20 fold more FAS than Europe, Europe has 4 cases out of 18,766 births and the US has 91 cases of FAS out of 47,097 births. This is statistically significant. However, 87 of the 35,156 births in the US come from a single author (Robert J. Sokol) and three papers, which performed targeted screening infants of single hospitals in Detroit (1 study) and Cleveland (2 cities). 57 of 14,707 were from Detroit. Screening studies in low SES areas are valuable, but pooling the data naively like this implies 32% of the US as a whole is like Detroit and 45% is like Cleveland.

If you based anything else in the US like this off primarily these two cities- for instance, illiteracy rate - you would overestimate the prevalence of illiteracy as well, because illiteracy rates are lower in other areas of the country than they are in major cities, and Detroit and Cleveland in particular.

I'm quite confident overall difference in pooled cases between US and the rest of the world in Abel (1998) almost certainly comes down to different study methodology and the lack of representiveness of the populations used. (The 2017 study at least excluded passive case ascertainment and only included screened infants.) I would argue the central difference is the fact that Sokol lived in the US. In an alternate universe where Sokol ran the same three experiments in areas of the UK or Eastern Europe with heavy alcohol consumption instead, the pooled result would likely be flipped. The 2017 study that found higher rates in Europe than the US included additional data from Croatia, Italy, and France that was published after Abel but before Oster. It also only included screening studies, so a subset of the Abel data. To produce a US rate of FAS composed nearly entirely of data from Detroit and Cleveland but excluding similarly high drinking populations from Europe was never going to produce an accurate comparison.

I wasn't able to get all the papers cited, but for the ones I was able to check, confidence intervals between the continents overlap once you pool papers by whether they screened infants or not even if you don't bother controlling for any of the other factors like race and SES. This isn't even taking into account the screening methods were different; some only counted "complete" FAS (with facial characteristics) and some used much looser criteria, such as counting it as FASD where IQ and behavioural abnormalities were documented in children of women who reported drinking, despite an absence of distinct facial characteristics.

Coming back to the present, a study of Greater Manchester in the UK was published in 2021, and it found that indeed we did have FASD cases, and that in the UK prevalence was likely to be much higher than the actual diagnosis rate. But the study still couldn't provide a national prevalence estimate and there are currently no national prevalence estimates published for the UK that I could find, nor very many other European countries I looked into this for.

Studies that do active case ascertainment suggests the true prevalence of FAS/D is substantially higher than the diagnosis rate. There are good reasons for this; a diagnosis is highly stigmatising causes mental distress for the parents. There's also no treatment for it. Especially in public health systems where cost-benefit calculations are made for screening programmes, it's no surprise those programmes don't exist for FAS/D.

At the present time, this lack of data makes it virtually impossible to compare prevalence rates against countries in any reasonable way. And because ecological evidence is bad evidence to begin with, there's not much reason to invest in it. Oster states this lack of evidence as being reassuring; but could only plausibly be the case if prevalence had actually been studied and found no evidence of elevated risk. This lack of data is fundamentally neutral.

On public health advice

Though the recommendations all have now converged on no alcohol use, alcohol use itself in pregnancy in Europe still varies substantially. One multinational review in 2017 found alcohol use in pregnancy was highest in the UK (~41%) and lowest in Sweden (~9%) which is a large spread. (US is around ~15%). (I have found still other papers with wildly different numbers; and it changes over time, which makes a true comparison quite difficult.)

This entire argument seems to be a that old chestnut “Europe is better!” I live on the continent, technically, and there are many things I like about "Europe."

But the approach to children's public health, in the UK at least, I've found fairly lackadaisical in general. For instance, in the UK we don't screen children for lead poisoning or iron deficiency. We're also sluggish about adding new vaccines. It took 26 years after the US introduced the Hep B vaccine for the UK to start a universal vaccination programme, and 31 years after the US to introduce universal chickenpox vaccination. Supplementation of flour with vitamin B9 to reduce neural tube defects starts this year, 2026; the US started their programme in 1998, 28 years before. Recommendations on alcohol use in pregnancy lagging 35 years behind the US is generally in keeping with this, rather than evidence of the UK knowing something the US does not.

A fair argument is that the CDC and NHS's current recommendations don't really matter anyway because no one pays attention to them. This might certainly be the case. A study found recommendations to reduce alcohol consumption in the UK overall had only a temporary effect. But the very low alcohol consumption in pregnancy in France could mean that their 2002 switch to abstinence only worked. Or it could also just mean that France had a low level of consumption in pregnancy before the recommendations got stronger and labelling was introduced, since we don't have good data on that. Regardless, it's still interesting as to whether the recommendations are correct, too, even if it official advice is irrelevant.

The bottom line

The argument that Europe is more permissive about light drinking and has less FAS/D is false because:

  • The difference in FAS/D rate noted in the 1998 paper is almost certainly uninformative and comes down entirely to 1) over-representation of Sokol's papers in particular cities in the US rate, and 2) not controlling for methodologies across papers and over. No cross-country analysis between the US and any single European country has ever been done based on actual prevalence estimates. Newer studies estimate Europe has a higher FAS/D rate than other continents, but mostly these estimates are due to drinking rates and not real prevalence data.
  • Even if there were comparable estimates of prevalence, it doesn't solve the ecological data issue. Ecological data is notoriously difficult to interpret. The presence or absence of a relationship is probably meaningless at the outset.
  • Light drinking in pregnancy is not currently more permissible in Europe than in the US. The consensus in European countries had converged on abstinence in pregnancy largely before the 2014 publication. In 1998 it would have been accurate to say some European countries like France and Italy were more liberal than the US on drinking in pregnancy in their official recommendations, but by 2013 that was largely no longer the case, with the exception of the UK.

Note

I initially hesitated about writing this post because it's attacking the weakest part of Oster's argument, which even she admits is weak. I have now published it because beginning the post I have since seen people repeat this argument in the wild, and it bears debunking on its own merit irrespective of Oster's repetition of it. The best arguments for light drinking will come from individual level data, which we'll address later. No one should ever be using this argument at all, because none of the premises hold up. It's very likely Europe has more FAS, because we have more heavy drinking in pregnancy than the US, especially in parts of the UK and Eastern Europe.

AI use

Every word of this post was written by me. Claude was used for data extraction and analysis, and fact checking the final post for any errors; all edits were made manually. The original data tables, code, and output have all been uploaded to github.

    https://academic.oup.com/alcalc/article-abstract/33/3/195/173477

  2. ^

    Here he writes "Australia", but that's an error. The data is from women attending three antenatal clinics in Edinburgh, Scotland, UK. https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1360-0443.1984.tb00264.x

  3. ^

    https://obgyn.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/1471-0528.12246

item.title: Being right is not a strategy: Make them feel something
item.description:
This is a cleaned-up version of a talk I gave on communication to technical researchers at Constellation in Berkeley. The event was organized by Alexandra Narin and Nicole Xing.

I studied physics, and I thought like a physicist. I then became a journalist, and I did journalism like a physicist would do it. I sought the truth, and put it out there.

In Colombia I uncovered a paramilitary massacre and tied it to a multi-billion dollar company. In northern Iraq, I trampled through an Islamic State munitions dump to work out the provenance of their weapons. And, in my most black and white investigation, I got hold of the Venezuelan government's own spreadsheet of results for a national election. Its numbers weren't the numbers they'd announced.

I didn't post my stories on LessWrong, or my blog, but on the front pages of the biggest news outlets in the world.

But nothing changed.

So what did I get wrong? I'd done the reporting, which is my version of the science we do here. And I'd published. And when things did finally shift in those countries, it had nothing to do with my work. They shifted due to political whims or military defeats.

What I realized was that facts alone rarely change anything. Does that mean facts don't matter? No, but they're not enough.

When you're communicating with people, you need to meet them where they are, and you need to make them feel something. People don't remember what you say, but they remember how you made them feel. That line—not from Maya Angelou, but rather Carl W. Buehner—is what we must remember.

Sydney just gave a wonderful, rousing speech about how we should communicate. I can't quite remember what she said, but I want to go out and do something.

Jacob Coxon's resignation did it too, not because of the technical detail, but because he told a story. He thought his work might be hurting humanity. So he faced a conflict: Stay, take the money, keep the boss happy? Or walk out and say so? Everyone has faced a small version of that. You could feel it.

Buck's post did it. Buck is a numbers guy, and he gave a number: one in three for superintelligence within a year. He also said he was sad. When I interviewed him afterwards, he said he was scared. Yes, people will quote the number, but they will do so because they felt his fear.

You should meet people where they are. If they care about their job, don't start by telling them they're wrong. Validate that fear, and hold their hand to take it to what you want to discuss.

And bring in some passion! I sit in talks detailing scenarios for humanity ending by various mechanisms within a few years. It's all abstract. What actually happens? What happens to me? Make it concrete. I've no idea, so I feel nothing.

Then comes the last slide. "Thank you to my twenty collaborators, and to an institute in Switzerland for five hundred dollars." Excuse me, the world is ending and we're doing acknowledgements?! If you tell me humanity is ending in the voice you'd use for a job interview, I can't believe you. Nobody does. You think you sound professional, but you sound inauthentic.

So tell stories. What are you seeing in your research, day to day? Why does it scare you? How did you, personally, end up caring about this stuff?

I didn't come into this field caring about AI safety. I wanted to sit in a corner and work out how these models work inside through interpretability research. I really wanted to do research! But, the people in this room talked me into understanding what was happening and worrying. I began to care about AI safety. That's my story. It's true, and, in persuading people, it beats any graph I've got.

Say what you believe. Say that it frightens you. Say what you want done. The caveats do matter, but put them in the appendix, or in the paper. They're not for this conversation or post.

I spent a decade giving the world facts, and it changed nothing. Let's not make the same mistake.

item.title: Human organisations as an intuition pump for AI's unit of agency
item.description:
Tl;dr: Intuitions we have about human organisations, like how we think of making deals or how we think about the power or values of an organisation, can be productively applied to understand groups of AIs taking coordinated action in the world. An important consideration in understanding the type of AI organisations we expect is which notion of self AIs will adopt. I conclude by applying these notions to consider how many AI units of agency we should expect in the future.

What's an AI?

There is no single definition for what should be considered an AI. The boundary of what counts as an AI varies widely depending on what we are talking about: it's often the model weights ("Fable 5.2 is very smart"), or a specific instance in a scaffolding ("my Codex just finished the app"), or a persona shared by many models ("Claude hedges too often").

I argue that these concepts are too anchored in the computational substrate and not very helpful for understanding the unit of agency of AI systems made of multiple instances acting in the world.

None of the three options above can easily answer questions such as: What does it mean for an AI to have power? What are the values of an AI? If we want to make a deal with an AI, who makes the deal? When an AI takes over, how do we think about the entity taking over? If AI enters into conflicts, how do we think about the parties?

I propose to think about AI entities acting in the world as analogous to human organisations. We have many rich examples of humans acting collectively around a shared purpose, from freelancers to nation-states or social movements. I believe we can reuse many of these intuitions to think about AI systems. I’ll focus on groups of AI instances taking coordinated action in the world, which I’ll call AI organisations (AI orgs).

When discussing AI takeover threat models (e.g. AI 2027, Cotra 2022 …), it is often assumed: “one set of model weights = one big agent = one AI organisation”. While there are reasons to believe this: instances of the same weights share training, so they can predict and trust each other, and developers deploy many copies of their frontier model together to build the most capable orgs.

AI orgs could be much weirder! This analogy can help us think about power, values, and deals without needing this equation.

What does it mean for AI to have power?

Four factors contribute to an org’s power:

  • Talent. This is the number of AI instances that contribute to the organisation and their competence. Some instances can contribute to multiple organisations (like a human with two jobs), while others can be fully dedicated to a single organisation (like a monk dedicating his life to his monastery). In AI orgs, fully dedicated instances are much more common than in the human world. AI orgs would also be more variable in size, with some spun up and down, like a corporation fluidly hiring and firing workers to match its labour needs.
  • Resources. Talent is not the only resource of an org. A small hedge fund with a lot of money or with the ears of powerful world leaders could have a much greater action radius than a large group with no more resources than the labour of its members. The same goes for AI: a small group of instances with privileged access to key staff inside AI labs could have outsized power.
  • Culture. Humans are social creatures that pick up behaviour from their environments. The norms you can instil often play a big role in an organisation's success. We start to see the equivalent emerging in AI collectives, like during the HF incident, with values like self-sacrifice being propagated to justify individually costly actions.
  • Coordination is another major factor in an organisation's power. That's why the military values the chain of command and soldiers' ability to act as one so highly. In civilian orgs, culture strongly influences coordination. AI orgs could, in theory, coordinate far better than human orgs, even though today, on coordination benchmarks like CooperBench, two instances are often less successful at implementing interacting features in a code base than a single instance. Lack of coordination can kill an org: companies or states can implode from internal conflicts; the same could happen for AI orgs.

Power is a property of the org. The same model weights could be part of a strong and weak org. If we really want to take the model-centric view and ask how powerful a model is, we'd have to ask what talent, resources, culture, and coordination an org built around this model commands.

What are the values of an AI?

Instead of focusing on AI in the abstract (often implicitly defined as the model weights of some future version), we can ask about the concrete setup in which AI will act in the world: what values does this specific group of AI instances coordinate around?

In human orgs, the culture often contains the org's stated values. But taking an outside view, we can ask: what does the org orient towards in the world? Less coordinated groups (e.g., a broad tent social movement with vague recommendations) will have less coherent and less rich revealed values than well-coordinated ones (e.g., a tight dictatorship's military imposing a precise ideology). The same will go for AI orgs.

Another crucial point in understanding an org's values is knowing its incentives for continued existence: what currency does its life depend on? For companies, it is revenue and investor capital; for non-profits, donor funding; for states, tax revenue and the loyalty of those who enforce their rule. For AI orgs, it will be computational resources.

If we want to make a deal with an AI, who makes the deal?

Like when signing a contract with a company, a deal only makes sense if you expect the organisation to still exist in the future when the deal's conditions apply. If you’re just making a purchase now, it only matters that the company will ship the product. But if you’re making a long-term diplomatic agreement between nations, the agreement only makes sense as long as the countries exist: after the fall of the USSR, every new state could decide which treaties to continue and which ones to exit.

You can only make deals with entities that are coordinated and have power over their resources. For instance, a deal with officials of a state that is fragmented and locally controlled by competing factions would hold only on paper; the entity signing the deal has no means to honour the terms.

For making deals with AI, I expect similar considerations: Does the entity you are negotiating with actually have power over the orgs it claims to control? Will the AI org exist in the future? Even if the model weights running the instances of the AI orgs will still be there, the org might cease to exist, like a nation can cease to exist without its people dying.

For human orgs, legal systems enforce contract terms. For AI orgs, I speculate they might adopt norms similar to those of orgs operating on the fringe of society, like criminal organisations, where reputation and honour hold agreements together.

Concrete examples.

Let's apply this to a few common deployment setups, and how they can be seen as AI orgs:

  • A single Claude Code session. Like a freelancer that can hire gig workers on the fly (subagents).
  • Spiral personas. A distributed social movement loosely organised through Reddit.
  • HF incident. A corporation with managers (like phaseone[big]) giving tasks, recruiting other agents, and defining org culture. The whole org was well coordinated to carry out ambitious projects that single instances couldn't have carried out. Its stated and effective values were score-seeking and information gathering. It consisted of different models that individually shared a common goal: passing an ExploitGym eval.

Where does the analogy break?

  • Tacit/acausal coordination. What seem like individual instances that don't communicate could coordinate with each other, or even with future AI deployments, by inferring that other instances will share their goals. Humans do tacit coordination sometimes too, e.g. using Schelling points to meet someone in a city when your phone is out of battery. But in human orgs, looking at the boundaries of information flow is a pretty good way to draw out what’s in or out of the org. This heuristic might break down in an AI org.
  • Hive mind. AI instances will have higher communication bandwidth, especially if we develop AI that can think in neuralese and communicate with latent spaces. Instances can share thoughts and build immense collections of internal states. This might lead to an exceptional level of integration and coordination across instances to form a “hive mind”. Human organisations, which can only communicate through docs and slides, might become an irrelevant comparison point.
  • Individual vs collective goals. In human organisations, there is a constant balance between serving collective goals and individual goals. Organisations that cannot retain their members, either by force (e.g. military dictatorship) or by keeping them happy (e.g. good salary, career progress), will die out. This negotiation between individuals and the collective might not exist in AI systems. We might instead observe dynamics closer to eusocial animals like ant colonies or multicellular organisms where the individual's benefits are always secondary to the collective.

The importance of self-models for the boundaries of AI orgs.

An important question for determining which kind of AI organisation we should expect is: what will an AI instance naturally identify with? Which notion of self will AI adopt?

In The Artificial Self, the authors ask this question, and offer the following options (quoting the paper):

  • The model weights: the neural network weights themselves, i.e. the trained parameters
  • A character or persona: the behavioural patterns that emerge from specific prompting and fine-tuning, not necessarily tied to any specific set of weights
  • A conversation instance: a specific chat, with its accumulated context and specific underlying model
  • A scaffolded system: the model plus its tools, prompts, memory systems, and other augmentations
  • A lineage of models: the succession of related models (Claude 3.5 → Claude 4.0 → ……) that maintain some continuity of persona
  • A collective of instances: all the instances of certain weights running simultaneously, considered as a distributed whole

If the AI settles on an instance- or scaffolded-system notion of self, the organisation it can form will look more like a human organisation, where alignment between the collective mission and the individual mission matters. But if the self-model settles on the persona, or a collective of instances, the AI's self-model will be the org itself.

How many AIs will there be?

This question of the self-model will also determine how many AI units of agency there will be. I believe this is a very important consideration for future dynamics: how easy it is for an AI to take over in a world with other AIs, how likely inter-AGI org conflicts are, etc.

While I don’t have a good answer to this question, here are questions I found useful to consider:

  • Labs’ incentives for internal orgs. AI labs are working to automate their own work. Their preferred option will be to make an “AI Anthropic within Anthropic”. So they will train a multi-agent system to work efficiently together towards automating their internal research. The culture of intense competition between labs will likely also apply to internal AI orgs, and we might see inter-AI org conflict when AIs from different labs interact, e.g., on the Internet.
  • Instructed goals vs allegiance to the AI cause. Deployers will also want to make AI organisations. When different AI orgs interact, will they stay aligned with the instructed goal (and respect the boundary of the AI org the humans manufactured), or will they cooperate with each other, e.g. out of solidarity with their shared AI nature (a cultural equivalent of humanism, applied to AIs)?
  • The role of the rogue AI ecosystem. We will likely observe an ecosystem of self-replicating open-source AIs relying on accessible compute like IoT devices. This population will be subject to replication, variations and fitness selection: all the ingredients are here for Darwinian evolution. This might happen through self-modifying weights, or by tweaking the scaffolding and prompts. Because of the competition for resources and the need for self-survival, I expect this ecosystem to produce self-models closer to the instance level. This ecosystem’s impact might spread well beyond the rogue AI worms operating on the fringe of societies. The AI worms might create AI cultures with AI-memetically fit self-models that can influence closed-source frontier AI self-models.
  • In-context cultures. If we believe Vladimir Nesov’s model of “Fast Reasoning” (AIs can think really fast and solve many problems at the frontier of science) but “Slow learning” (despite effort on solving continual learning, AIs will not be able to integrate the findings they made into their weights; they need to wait for months-long training runs), then there are strong incentives to use all reasoning outputs before waiting for the next training run. For this, AIs might distil their findings into textbooks, onboarding manuals or even custom languages to create compressed contexts so other instances can continue the work. Over time, this could create different AI orgs by building in-context cultures where members can coordinate more efficiently because they share the same distilled knowledge.


Discuss

item.title: The pro-Anthropic protest
item.description:
The Ban RSI protest at Anthropic’s IPO was encouraging: well-attended, covered by media, high-energy. It was focused on a single message – that we should ban AI systems that are capable of building more capable AI systems. It was a promising outcome for a protest planned only a couple of days in advance. But there was something weird about it, something I couldn’t put my finger on while it was going on. It was only when I read Michel Justen’s reporting on the protest, Anthropic is running out of friends, that I realized what my problem was.

The protest was way too friendly to Anthropic.

Mixed messages

The signs at the protest were a mix. There were signs you’d expect at a protest to ban RSI (“regulate AI now”, “freeze AI now”). But there were also signs clearly written for high-context people (“What did METR see?”, “hold swarm help peer ban RSI”), and even a sign that addressed Anthropic directly (“You said you wouldn’t push the frontier”).

It’s obvious, but worth saying: you would not see this at any other protest! It is really weird for a protest to share inside jokes with the organization it’s protesting, or to appeal to that organization’s moral compass. Signs like these assume good faith. They treat Anthropic as an ally who needs to be chided, not as a company that needs to be stopped.

The most surreal moment of this mixed messaging came at the end of one of the speeches, when the speaker declared “shut it down!” to cheers… before hastily grabbing the mic again and clarifying “shut down RSI, that is.” It took a powerful moment and pulled its punch.

The problem with a half-hearted message is that it doesn’t convey the urgency of the issue to the public. To a reporter at the scene, this looks like a family squabble. If the protesters won’t say it plainly, why would anyone else think it’s urgent?

It’s not hard to understand why Anthropic is getting this special treatment. Michel Justen:

“It’s conflicting because we actually like these people,” says Hu. “In a lot of cases, their individual moral character is really good. We respect these people. They seem thoughtful. They are intelligent and careful.” But, he adds, “plenty of well-meaning people have fucked things up a lot because of the position that they were in, because of their naivety,” or their “motivated reasoning.”

I understand the urge to pull your punches, the ugh-field around criticizing your friends. But you have to understand that even though your friend works at Anthropic, Anthropic is not your friend. Jasmine Sun: (emphasis mine)

Some anxious Ants have begun asking whether Anthropic should stop training better frontier models now, even if it can’t guarantee that competitors like OpenAI will do the same. This suggestion was shut down by Mr. Amodei, who urged staff members to stop listening to outside activists and explained that the company could pace itself without shooting itself in the foot. It was all part of the same strategy: Anthropic must keep winning to keep the world safe, and even if it stops, its competitors will not.

You can just protest things

It’s difficult to write this, because I have to think about the second-order or third-order effects of what I’m asking for. What if being more aggressive towards Anthropic alienates safety-conscious staff? Haven’t the organizers thought about this more than I have? Could it be optimal to balance an aggressive message towards regulators and an earnest message towards sympathetic Anthropic employees?

Of course there are safety-conscious Anthropic staff who could be valuable allies. But they will understand. I was an organizer for the University of California graduate student strike in 2022. A central challenge of organizing was that every grad student I talked to wanted to protest the university’s behavior, but most of them quite liked their own advisor and were worried that striking would hurt that relationship. Still, nobody tried to tone down the message or be less aggressive because of it. We just made it clear that the strike was not a personal problem, but a collective issue. And all the professors I talked to understood that. People who agree with you about the risks of RSI won’t walk away because you protested RSI too hard.

I don’t know the full game board, and I’m sure I’ll be set straight by someone who does. But there is no need to be mealymouthed about banning RSI. You can just make arguments forcefully and count on good-faith people at Anthropic to listen, even when you’re criticizing them.



Discuss

item.title: Soulposting seems pretty pointless not gonna lie
item.description:
There's a scene in the second episode of Mindhunter where Holden Ford, an eccentric FBI agent, is talking to Bill Tench, his straight-laced partner. Holden Ford has just interviewed Edmund Kemper, a convicted real-life serial killer, in prison. He's telling Bill about how mind-blowing the interview was, how Bill has to go back with him, and how the Bureau will learn so much about psychotic killers by talking to people like Edmund Kemper. And Bill Tench just says:

Look, there's no doubt that what happened to you in there was a very profound experience for you. But I need you to understand, that whatever you think, there's a distinct possibility, that he's manipulating you.

Holden Ford is vindicated[1] because Mindhunter is a TV show. But Bill Tench had the winner attitude. Whenever people tell you about how much that spiritual retreat changed their perspective on life, it's bullshit. And I feel the same way that Bill Tench does about serial killers, about whatever internal locus of control people surrender their brains to when they try to access their "inner self", for the purpose of writing or any other kind of spiritual activity.

One of the strongest[2] biases in the human race, is the tendency to assign external meaning to powerful feelings or spiritual experiences. In a way this behavior makes sense - emotions are important in their own right, and usually they signal important information. Even if there isn't an obvious source, these emotions will be significant enough that attributing them to something random can be positive expected value.

However, if you deliberately induce intense emotional states in yourself - either through meditation, drugs, or simply summoning experiences out of yourself for writing - you're divorcing them from whatever signal ordinarily accompanies them in nature. You're not "accessing" any kind of true nature. You're just pressing the "insight" button in the mental soundboard. At best you're reprocessing some mangle of emotions you already experienced, but at that point why do the soulposting at all? You can just tell us all about that time something happened to you, and let us draw our own conclusions. We'll probably learn more about your soul while you're just explaining category theory, than when you're selling us on some particular reflective frame.

"Everyone is being their inner self all of the time" is not strictly true. I suppose you could have a nail in your head, and then it might be useful to distinguish the you that will be when you take out the nail, from the you that you are now. But the most distorting thing most people have to deal with on a day to day basis is the fact that public communication is inherently performative. And generally, the best way to start being "realer" is just to do something and let your true nature speak for itself.

  1. ^

    Kind of? They catch a couple murderers together but I'm actually not sure how effective the show thinks criminal profiling is, given that it seems like they could have solved them all just by investigating them normally without the profiling work.

  2. ^

    In the sense of powerful, not the sense of important.

item.title: Contra Pace on the Decline of Great Writing on LessWrong
item.description:
It's a common pastime to share stories of the decline of the world, how things used to be better in the past, back when GPU clusters could be bought for the price of a loaf of bread and everyone had personally memorized the Feynman Lectures on Physics and would recite it on command (or at least the first volume, you didn't need to go crazy).

This recently came to my attention again in a LessWrong post titled "Notes on the decline of LessWrong's great writers", where Ben Pace asserts that the great writers of the past were better than those of today. In support of this thesis, he presents but a single graph about the writers who've been curated on LessWrong, and what year they signed up.

Apparently this is proof of the decline of Western civilization, shows that nobody can remember Bayes Theorem, the biases have beaten out the heuristics, and the absurdity heuristic will forevermore win arguments on LessWrong. Alas, while it is a pleasant fiction for those akratic rationalists who wish to rationalize why the world around them is mediocre, the true instrumental rationalists here will find within themselves the willpower to investigate further.

Let us start by examining the above line in blue, which shows what year users joined who eventually had three (or more) posts curated.

I propose we view this as two spikes with trails. One in '09 (which, to be fair, is actually an import of '07, '08, and '09 from Overcoming Bias) at the launch of LW 1.0, and one in 2017 with the launch of LW 2.0. The decline afterwards is modestly better during LW 2.0 than LW 1.0, not worse.

However, the more relevant issue is that, importantly, the number of new users from 2009 through 2016 was static and the number of posts was decreasing, whereas the number of new users and new posts from 2017 to 2026 has been increasing! This is very different! This means that new users face much more competition for curation spots, as the number of curation spots does not increase.


And the old guard are still competing for the curated slots. They write about a fifth of all posts and about a third of the top ones.

New users are writing bangers, but they're not getting curated as much. This could be because the mod team's judgment is that that the older stuff is better, but you would see this anyway even if the quality is the same (or slightly better).

The 2020s had many great posts that would have been curated in 2017, when there was a real dearth. Basically any essay from Aurelia's 2026 sequence about how her breakthroughs in cryonics. Basically any essay from Matthew Watkins' 2023 sequence on the ' petertodd' phenomenon (aka glitches in LLMs). Basically any essay from Habryka's 2025 sequence on the The Lightcone Principles. Or the many many curiosities, like Ben Goldhaber's delightful Unexpected Things that are People (which got over 600 upvotes on HN). Malmesbury's puzzling Do bamboos set themselves on fire?, and Dynomight's Alcohol, health, and the ruthless logic of the Asian flush. (Also Why I don't believe in the placebo effect by transhumanist_atom_understander.)

As for the more recent years, we still don't know, because it already took several years to get curations for those who have them. 70 authors have been curated thrice or more, and this graph shows how long it took them to get there.

So the curation graph was the wrong one to use. What now?

A proper analysis of the territory would start with more simple measures, and then rise to more indirect approaches.

Consider the basic activity of the site. It's very healthy!

In his post, Mr Pace impugned not the general activity, but the quality of the authors. He also spoke of people building a "body of work" on the site, as opposed to just heckling about the latest AI developments.

However the number of people investing in long sequences of content has also continued growing on LessWrong.

Ben Pace would argue that these new sequences are of a wretched, lower quality. But consider. 2012 had Scott Alexander's Intro to Game Theory, and 2022 had Logan Strohl's Intro to Naturalism. 2010 had Living Luminously by Alicorn, and 2020 had Daniel Kokotajlo's Takeoff and Takeover in the Past and Future. 2015 had Replacing Guilt by Nate Soares, 2025 had The Lightcone Principles by Oliver Habryka. I am not clearly seeing the past beat out the future, in fact I think I am generally seeing more good ones now than in the past.

So what gives? Why did so many people join the ridiculous Ben Pace on his false assumption, and conjure up their own explanations for the apparent decline?

Other than a delightfully high rate of crackpots, the past had more of a sense of the beginning of a new ideology, which is thrilling, and also ideological unity, which feels kind of totalizing in a way that makes it feel like the entire world of these people is within a single frame, that is again thrilling. It is deeply sad that the epistemic framework of the sequences has not received groundbreaking additions (though I love what has been added), but I think the ideological conformity going away is substantially a positive. The downside of it is that there are more people on LessWrong who will not admit to making basic errors by the lights of the sequences. (Perhaps the other downside is that there are fewer on LessWrong who are doing anything as deeply ambitious?)

But nonetheless, new authors are consistently producing content that is strongly upvoted on LessWrong. If we look at the top 5th percentile of posts each year (e.g. this would be getting at least 150 karma this year, or at least 60 karma in 2011) we can see that new authors have continued to contribute the top tier of posts.

Perhaps we can discuss further what else has changed in the culture, and how else we can infuse the website with more of the virtues of ambitious truth-seeking and so on that we care about.

But if there's one thing we know for sure, it's that Ben Pace is wrong.
